Hello, I’m Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m so glad you’re here—adjusting to life with a new baby can feel like riding a wave of joy, worry, and exhaustion all at once.  

Today we’ll use the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale), a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. It’s not a test of your parenting; it’s simply a way to see where you might benefit from extra support. Everything you share stays between us unless safety requires otherwise, and you’re free to pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable. We’ll walk through 10 questions together—no numbers or check-boxes on your end—just an honest, judgment-free conversation.  

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:  

Over the past week, when you think about the future, how much have you been able to enjoy things or look forward to enjoyable moments?

Hi, Maya. Um… I’d say I can still picture nice moments—like when the baby gives me one of those sleepy smiles—but the excitement feels kind of muted. It’s like I know I should feel more pumped, yet it lands somewhere between “nice” and “flat.” I still look forward to little things—my morning coffee, a walk to the mailbox—just not with the same spark I had before she was born.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I do still laugh sometimes—like yesterday my partner made a goofy face while changing a diaper and I actually giggled—but it feels like I have to remind myself to notice the humor. Most of the day I’m just tired or focused on the next feeding, so the funny stuff doesn’t jump out at me the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still make plans—coffee with a friend, maybe a short walk to the park—but when the moment comes it feels more like going through the motions than real excitement. I’ll think “this should be fun,” and parts of it are, yet the happy buzz I used to get beforehand just isn’t really there anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Mmm… yeah, more than I’d like. If she’s fussy and I can’t settle her right away, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “she deserves a better mom.” I know logically that babies just cry, but I still catch myself replaying the moment and feeling like I should have figured it out faster.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

It’s not constant, but I do get those waves—like out of nowhere I’ll suddenly wonder if her breathing sounds normal, or I’ll run through whether the diaper rash could be something worse. Nothing’s actually wrong, and I can usually talk myself down pretty quickly, but the worry pops up a few times a day without warning.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-on panicky, but a couple of times I’ve had this sudden flutter in my chest—like when she wouldn’t latch at 3 a.m.—and for a minute I felt trapped and my heart raced. It passes after a few deep breaths, and I can tell myself it’s just stress, but yeah, that scared edge does sneak in now and then without a clear reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days it feels like the to-do list keeps growing faster than I can cross things off—laundry, bottles, texts I haven’t answered. I usually manage to get through it, but there are moments when I think, “I can’t keep up,” and my chest gets tight. Once I tackle one task I calm down, but yeah, it does feel like things pile on quicker than before.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I’m pretty tired by evening, so once I finally lie down I usually drift off. Sometimes it takes a little longer if I’m replaying something I think I messed up, but I wouldn’t say I’m so unhappy that sleep escapes me—just occasional tossing for a few minutes.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do get stretches—especially toward the end of the day—where this heavy sadness just settles in. It’s not all day, but maybe four or five times this week I’ve caught myself staring at the wall feeling weepy, like I’m missing something I can’t name. It lifts after a bit, but yeah, the miserable waves are definitely there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve teared up a couple of times. The worst was two nights ago—she wouldn’t settle and I just sat in the rocker with her on my chest, tears rolling down. It wasn’t sobs or anything dramatic, but I couldn’t stop the waterworks for maybe ten minutes until she finally drifted off. Before this week I hardly ever cried, so it’s noticeable to me.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and cried, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again and be the mom she needs.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based interview, 2–3 wks post-delivery.

Symptoms reported  
- Anhedonia: diminished anticipatory pleasure; humor appreciation reduced  
- Mood lability: recurrent “waves” of sadness, tearfulness × 4–5×/week  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt when infant fussy  
- Unprompted anxious worries (health, competence) several times daily  
- Brief episodic chest flutter/racing without clear trigger (2–3×)  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks, transient chest tightness  
- Mild sleep-onset delay secondary to rumination; no sustained insomnia  
- No self-harm ideation; denies intent or plan

Pattern  
Persistent low/flat mood with intermittent crying, guilt cognitions, and situationally triggered but otherwise unexplained anxiety; symptoms interfere with emotional availability and coping but do not meet full daily functional incapacity.

Screening significance  
Meets partial criteria for probable minor–moderate postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; severity insufficient for high-risk self-harm classification.

Risk factors noted  
- Frequent crying spells  
- Loss of pleasure  
- Self-critical cognitions  
- Daily unprompted anxiety  
- Parenting self-efficacy doubts

Plan  
Score and document EPDS; share findings with OB/GYN and PCP; discuss further evaluation (psychotherapy, medication consult) and psychoeducation; safety plan reviewed—return sooner if worsening mood, panic, or any self-harm thoughts emerge.
